name: Laurence Brown Douglas
story: Laurence Brown Douglas is the man at the center of this book. He was born at nine o'clock on the evening of June 14, 1907, at the Royal Maternity Hospital in Lauriston Place, Edinburgh. Twenty days later his mother, Agnes Brown, a domestic servant, registered him as Lawrence Brown. The column for his father's name was left blank, and the word Illegitimate was written under his name. For her home she gave Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar.

By the spring of 1911 he was living at 16 Lochrin Place in Edinburgh as Laurence B. Douglas, the son of the house of Robert and Elizabeth Douglas. In 1912 the family moved to Dunfermline, where a school clerk wrote one word beside his name: Adopted. He grew up there with the Douglases' daughter, Janet. Robert Douglas died of tuberculosis in 1919, and in October 1920, at thirteen, Laurence left school with an exemption and went to work as a message boy for a grocer.

In September 1929 he sailed from Greenock with Janet on the Duchess of Bedford and crossed into the United States at Detroit as Lawrence Brown, twenty-two, grocer, six feet tall, fair hair, blue eyes, fifty dollars. In Chicago he lodged with Janet and her husband. In September 1930 he married Helen Ena Harrison, a soldier's daughter from Ayr. By 1937 he was in Providence as a display man, dressing store windows on Weybosset Street, the trade he would follow for the rest of his life. Helen later divorced him.

In October 1939 he married Constance Eugenie Darcy in Birmingham, Alabama. They lived in San Francisco, where he dressed the windows of Bond Stores, and in 1943, in a federal court in Pittsburgh, he became an American citizen as Laurence Brown Douglas: both names at once. After the war the family settled in Pawtucket and then Providence, at 644 River Avenue. He died at St. Joseph's Hospital in Providence on March 9, 1961, at fifty-three, and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston. His grandson, Doug Garceau, wrote this book.

name: Agnes McGarth Brown
story: Agnes McGarth Brown was Laurence's mother. She was born at half past two in the afternoon on December 18, 1885, in a ploughman's cottage at Edston, near Peebles, the second daughter of George Brown and Christina Henderson. Her father gave her his own mother's name, Agnes McGarth. He died when she was three and a half months old, and her mother took the two girls home to Libberton parish, to the row of cottages at Quothquan.

Her mother died in February 1891, when Agnes was five, and her grandmother, Jane Henderson, took her in. That June her grandmother died too. Agnes grew up in the cottage later called Lime Tree, with her sister Mary, her uncle Andrew Henderson and James Parker, the boy her grandmother had raised. A few doors along lived Mary Archibald, whose brother Alexander would become the gardener at Shieldhill House.

By 1907 she was a domestic servant. In the autumn of 1906 she became pregnant. Her home was no longer her uncle's house but Gean Cottage, where Mary Archibald lived, and it was Gean Cottage she gave as her home when she registered her son, Lawrence Brown, in Edinburgh on July 4, 1907. The column for the father's name was left blank.

By 1911 she was a nurse at the Royal Edinburgh Asylum in Morningside. On August 28, 1911, she married an asylum attendant, Thomas McKay McKenzie, by declaration at Chambers Street, before the same registrar who had recorded her son's birth. They had two daughters, Mary Christina in 1912 and Jean Henderson in 1914. One portrait of her is known. Where and when she died has not yet been found.

name: George Brown
story: George Brown was Laurence's grandfather, the father of Agnes. He was born on July 18, 1862, one of at least ten children of William Brown, a ploughman, and Agnes McGarth, and he became a ploughman like his father. In 1871 the census found him at eight in the same household as his elder brother Lawrence Tweedie Brown.

On Friday, June 1, 1883, at twenty, he married Christina Henderson at Quothquan, in the parish of Libberton. Their first daughter, Mary Henderson Brown, was born that August. By the winter of 1885 George had found work at Edston, a farm in the parish of Lyne near Peebles, and there his second daughter, Agnes McGarth Brown, was born on December 18, 1885. He registered her himself on the last day of the year and signed as her father.

George Brown died at Edston at half past one in the morning on April 5, 1886, aged twenty-three, when Agnes was three and a half months old. His death register is the document that names his own parents. His widow took their two girls home to Libberton.

name: Christina Henderson Brown
story: Christina Henderson was Laurence's grandmother, the mother of Agnes. She was born on March 19, 1860, at Libberton, the eldest child of Alexander Henderson and Jane Robb, and grew up in the farm country under Quothquan Law, four miles from Biggar.

She married George Brown, a ploughman, at Quothquan on June 1, 1883. Eleven weeks later she gave birth to their first daughter, Mary, and went to the registrar herself. Her second daughter, Agnes, was born at Edston near Peebles in December 1885. Four months later George died, and Christina, a widow at twenty-six, took the two girls home to Libberton.
Christina died at Quothquan on February 10, 1891, at thirty, eight weeks before the census found her daughters in their grandmother's cottage. Her name is cut into the Henderson family stone.

name: William Brown
story: William Brown was Laurence's great-grandfather on his mother's side. He was a ploughman in the sheep country of Peeblesshire, born about 1835, who walked behind a pair of horses turning the ground for oats and turnips and moved from farm to farm as the term days dictated. Like most farm laborers of his time, he owned no land and no house; the cottage came with the job.

He married Agnes McGarth of Tweedsmuir. They had at least ten children: William, about 1859; Lawrence Tweedie, 1860; George, 1862; then Alexander, Jane, John, James Tweedie, Agnes, Thomas and Tweedie McGarth Brown. The McGarth and Tweedie names were passed down as middle names for three generations.
Two of his sons matter to this story. George was the father of Agnes McGarth Brown, Laurence's mother. Lawrence Tweedie Brown was the uncle whose first name Agnes gave her son.

name: Agnes McGarth
story: Agnes McGarth was Laurence's great-grandmother, the wife of William Brown. She was born about 1840 at Tweedsmuir, where the Tweed rises in the hills of Peeblesshire. In 1851 the census found her in her parents' crowded house: her father, Tweedie McGarth; her mother, Jane, a woman from Wamphray in Dumfriesshire; and her brothers and sisters Jane, James Tweedie, Sarah, Ann and Janet.

She married William Brown, a ploughman, and raised at least ten children. Her son George named his second daughter for her, Agnes McGarth Brown, and so her name came down to Laurence's mother. More than a century later an indexer misread it as McGrath, but the handwriting in the register says McGarth.

lineage.who: William, Lawrence Tweedie, George and at least seven more

name: Lawrence Tweedie Brown
story: Lawrence Tweedie Brown was the elder brother of George Brown and the uncle of Agnes McGarth Brown. He was born on September 14, 1860, at Peebles, a son of William Brown and Agnes McGarth. In 1871 the census found him at ten in the same household as his brother George.
He married Isabella Graham of Cambusnethan, raised a family at Traquair and Sanquhar, and eventually settled in Quebec, where he died in 1943.

His place in this story is his name. When Agnes registered her son in 1907, she gave him the first name Lawrence, the name of her father's elder brother. In the family it was understood that the boy was named for him.

name: Mary Henderson Brown
story: Mary Henderson Brown was Agnes's elder sister, and Laurence's aunt. She was born at Quothquan at twenty past eight on the morning of August 18, 1883, eleven weeks after her parents' wedding, and her mother registered her herself.

Her father died when she was two and a half, and her mother when she was seven. In April 1891 the census found her, seven, and Agnes, five, in their grandmother Jane Henderson's cottage in the Castle row. In 1901, at seventeen, she was still at Lime Tree Cottage with Agnes, their uncle Andrew Henderson and James Parker. She was the one member of her own family who grew up beside Agnes from the start.

name: Jane Henderson
story: Jane Henderson, born Jane Robb, was Agnes's grandmother, and Laurence's great-grandmother. She was a crofter born at Carnwath, the wife of Alexander Henderson, and she raised her family at Libberton: Christina, Jane, Janet, David and, about 1876, a late son, Andrew.

Hers was a house that took children in. In 1881 she was raising a boy of eight, James Parker, entered in the census as her Adopted Son. In February 1891 her daughter Christina died, and Jane took in Christina's two girls, Mary and Agnes Brown. On census night that April she was fifty-six, at the fifth cottage of the row called Castle, with her daughter Jane, her son Andrew, James Parker and her two granddaughters.
She died on June 8, 1891, four months after her daughter. Her cottage, later called Lime Tree, remained Agnes's home until Agnes moved a few doors along to Gean Cottage.

lineage.who: Christina (Brown), Jane, Janet, David and Andrew Henderson
Mary Henderson Brown and Agnes McGarth Brown

name: Andrew Henderson
story: Andrew Henderson was Agnes's uncle, her mother's younger brother. He was the late son of Alexander Henderson and Jane Robb, a boy of five in his mother's cottage in 1881 and a schoolboy of fourteen in 1891, when his orphaned nieces came to the house.

By March 1901 he was twenty-five, a groom who worked with horses, and the head of the household at Lime Tree Cottage. With him were his nieces, Mary and Agnes Brown, and a boarder, James Parker. Agnes depended on him for the roof over her head. Long after he was gone the village remembered "Andrew Henderson, late of Lime Tree" as a poet and a keeper of bees. His whereabouts after 1901 have not been traced.

name: Thomas McKay McKenzie
story: Thomas McKay McKenzie was the man Agnes Brown married, four years after her son was born. In 1911 he was an asylum attendant at West House, the Royal Edinburgh Asylum in Morningside, where Agnes was a nurse. His father was John Alexander McKenzie, a coastguardsman, and his mother, Mary McKay, had died.

They married by declaration at 34 Chambers Street, Edinburgh, on August 28, 1911. He was twenty-one; Agnes was twenty-five. Their daughters, Mary Christina and Jean Henderson McKenzie, were born in 1912 and 1914. On December 9, 1915, Thomas attested for the army, giving his work as barman and his family's address as 62 Balcarres Street, Morningside. He served at home from 1916 to 1919. There was no son on his family form.

lineage.who: Mary Christina McKenzie, 1912; Jean Henderson McKenzie, 1914

name: Mary and Jean McKenzie
story: Mary Christina McKenzie and Jean Henderson McKenzie were Laurence's half-sisters, the daughters of Agnes Brown and Thomas McKay McKenzie. Mary was born at ten in the morning on May 6, 1912, at 9 Stewart Terrace, Edinburgh. Jean was born in Edinburgh in August 1914, the month the war began, and carried the surname of Agnes's mother's people.

In December 1915 their father's army papers listed them with their mother at 62 Balcarres Street, Morningside. Across the Firth of Forth, in Dunfermline, their half-brother was growing up as Laurence Douglas. No record yet found names them together.

name: Alexander Archibald
story: Alexander Archibald was the gardener of Shieldhill, and the man this book believes took Agnes Brown in. He was the son of a widow, Ann Archibald, born Ann Purves, and the brother of Mary and John. In April 1891, at twenty, he lived in the row of cottages called Castle at Quothquan and broke stones for the county roads. That spring Agnes, five, came to live in her grandmother's cottage a few doors along.

That June his brother John died at eighteen, twelve days after Agnes's grandmother. In December 1897 his mother died, and at about the same time his sister Mary had a daughter of her own, with no marriage the records show.

In 1898 Nathaniel Dunlop bought Shieldhill. By census night in 1901 the stonebreaker had become the domestic gardener at the big house. The laird was away, and the household living in Shieldhill House was the gardener's: Alexander, thirty, his wife, Annie, twenty-six, born at Carnwath, and a dairymaid.

When Agnes was carrying a child in the autumn of 1906, Alexander took her to his sister's house, Gean Cottage. There Mary Archibald kept her through the pregnancy, and when Agnes came home from the hospital in Edinburgh she brought her son back to Gean Cottage, where he spent his earliest days. No record yet found says whether Alexander was still the gardener at Shieldhill in 1906.

homes.label: Shieldhill House, where he was the gardener
Gean Tree Cottage, his sister's house

name: Mary Archibald
story: Mary Archibald was the woman who took Agnes Brown into her home. She was born on October 23, 1864, at Libberton, the daughter of George Archibald and Ann Purves, and grew up in the row of cottages at Quothquan. When Agnes, five, came to her grandmother's cottage in 1891, Mary was a grown woman a few doors along, one of the first Agnes knew outside her own family.

In 1891 her brother John died, and in December 1897 her mother. At about the same time Mary had a daughter of her own, Annie P. R., who lived until 1992. No record yet found shows that Mary was married when her daughter was born. In 1901 she was a sewing mistress living alone at Gean Tree; her daughter, about three, was not with her. Her brother Alexander was the gardener at Shieldhill House.

When Agnes was pregnant in the autumn of 1906, she left her uncle's house of men at Lime Tree and moved in with Mary at Gean Cottage. Mary kept her through the winter and spring, a roof, a fire and food on the table when Agnes could no longer earn them, and it was her house Agnes named as home when she registered her son. By 1911 Mary was gone from Gean Tree. She later married John Cuthbertson, who is named on her gravestone at Biggar.

name: Ann Archibald
story: Ann Archibald, born Ann Purves, was the mother of Mary, Alexander and John Archibald. In April 1891 she was fifty-four, a widow and a crofter, living in the third cottage of the row called Castle at Quothquan, two doors from Jane Henderson, with her three children and a visitor, Isabella Purves.

Her son John, a farm servant, died on June 20, 1891, at eighteen. Ann died on December 10, 1897, and her name is cut on the Archibald family stone at Libberton. Her children Mary and Alexander are at the heart of what happened to Agnes Brown in 1906 and 1907.

name: James Lawson Parker
story: James Parker was the boy Jane Henderson raised as her own. He was born at Biggar about 1872, and in 1881, at eight, the census entered him in her cottage as "Adopted Son." In 1891 he was still there, eighteen, an agricultural laborer, when Agnes, five, came to the house. He was thirteen years older than she was, something between an uncle and an older brother.

In 1901 he was twenty-eight, a gamekeeper, boarding at Lime Tree Cottage with Andrew Henderson and his two nieces. On August 28, 1903, at Coldstream, in the parish of Carluke, he married Janet Crawford Stewart, a shepherd's daughter, and signed his full name: James Lawson Parker. He named his parents as Benjamin Parker, a mason, and Jane Lawson, a lady's maid, both dead. A boy called James Lawson was registered at Biggar in 1872, which suggests he began life under his mother's name.

He brought his wife home to Shieldhill. In 1911 he was thirty-eight, a gamekeeper at 3 Shieldhill Mains, with Janet and three children, John, Euphemia and Robert. No record says anything about his conduct toward Agnes, and this book does not suggest it.

name: Sir Nathaniel Dunlop
story: Nathaniel Dunlop owned the Shieldhill estate when Laurence was born. He was born at Campbeltown on April 7, 1830, served the Allan Line, the Glasgow shipping company whose steamers carried tens of thousands of Scottish emigrants to Canada, for half a century, and was chairman of the Clyde Navigation Trust.

In 1898 he bought Shieldhill from the Chancellor family, and with it the village of Quothquan and its cottages. He rebuilt houses in the village, and in 1903 he and his daughter, Ellen, put up Shieldhill Hall for evening services. He had been a widower since 1867. On June 28, 1907, two weeks after Laurence's birth, his name was in the King's birthday honours, and on July 15 he was knighted at Buckingham Palace as Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill, Biggar.

He died at Shieldhill on November 15, 1919. His will names his daughter, nephews and nieces, his household staff and charities. No Agnes Brown, Lawrence or Laurence, Douglas or Archibald is named in it.

name: Ellen Dunlop
story: Ellen Dunlop was the only daughter of Nathaniel Dunlop, the owner of Shieldhill. In 1903 she and her father put up Shieldhill Hall in the village of Quothquan, a hall of corrugated iron with timber gables, for evening services. It still stands.

She took a close interest in the running of the Shieldhill estate, where her father was often away in Glasgow. Alexander Archibald was the domestic gardener at the house in 1901. Her father's will of 1919 left gifts to the household servants as she might direct.

name: Shieldhill Estate and House
story: Shieldhill was the estate on the hill above the village of Quothquan, in the parish of Libberton in Upper Clydesdale, four miles from Biggar. Its house was a rambling mansion built around an old tower, with stonework of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and additions of about 1820. With the estate came the village and its cottages, among them the row the census of 1891 called Castle, where Agnes Brown grew up.

The Chancellor family held the lands of Shieldhill from 1434, when George Chancellor was granted them with part of Quothquan. Shieldhill became the family's main home after their house at Quothquan was destroyed, following William Chancellor's support for Mary Queen of Scots at the Battle of Langside. The family buried their dead in the ruined old kirk at Quothquan, which they had taken as a family burial place around 1780. In 1898 they sold Shieldhill to Nathaniel Dunlop, a Glasgow shipowner of the Allan Line. Dunlop rebuilt Huntfield Place, turning six houses into four, enlarged the smith's house, and in 1903, with his daughter, Ellen, put up Shieldhill Hall in the village for evening services.

On census night in 1901 the house stood nearly empty. The laird was away at his house in Govan, and the household living in Shieldhill House was the gardener's: Alexander Archibald, thirty, his wife, Annie, and a dairymaid, Susan Cumisky. The estate was kept by its resident staff, servants, gardeners and keepers. A few doors down the hill, at Gean Tree, lived the gardener's sister, Mary Archibald, and at Lime Tree lived Agnes Brown, fifteen.

Shieldhill is the place at the center of Laurence's beginning. When Agnes registered her son in Edinburgh in July 1907, she gave her home as Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar. That same month the King knighted the estate's owner as Sir Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill. In 1911 James Parker, the boy Agnes grew up beside, was the gamekeeper at Shieldhill Mains. Dunlop died at Shieldhill on November 15, 1919.

The house is still there, a category B listed building whose oldest surviving part is a sixteenth-century square keep. It became a country house hotel in 1959 and reopened in August 2020 after a long refurbishment. In 1997 Nelson Mandela stayed there during the Commonwealth summit in Edinburgh and planted an oak tree in the grounds. In 2026 Shieldhill was bought by Mike and Ross Baxter, the Edinburgh brothers who founded the House of Gods hotels.

name: Robert Douglas
story: Robert Douglas was the man who raised Laurence. He was born at 9 Canon Street, Edinburgh, on May 8, 1876, the son of Archibald Douglas, then a traveller for a wood merchant and later a forester, and Isabella Gray. On June 9, 1899, at twenty-three, a saw miller, he married Elizabeth Millar McDonald at 34 St Patrick Square by the forms of the Free Church of Scotland. Within two years he was a stone machineman, a skilled worker who cut and dressed stone by machine.

Their daughter, Janet Page Douglas, was born on April 29, 1900. Family information says a second daughter, Isabella Gray Douglas, died as an infant. By April 1911 the boy born Lawrence Brown was living in their home at 16 Lochrin Place as Laurence B. Douglas, their son. In 1912 the family moved to Dunfermline, and the school register named Robert as the boy's guardian.

Robert had had lupus, tuberculosis of the skin, since he was a boy, and in his last year it reached his lungs. He died at Woodburn Sanatorium in Morningside, Edinburgh, on September 9, 1919, aged forty-three. Laurence was twelve.

name: Elizabeth Millar McDonald (Lizzie Douglas)
story: Elizabeth Millar McDonald, known as Lizzie, was the woman who raised Laurence, and the mother he named in every record that asked. She was born at Liberton, on the southern edge of Edinburgh, on May 31, 1874. Her mother, Ann McDonald, was about twenty and unmarried, and no father is named. In 1878 Ann married and sailed for New Zealand, leaving Lizzie, four, with her grandparents, John and Janet McDonald, at Gilmerton.

She went into service at sixteen. On June 9, 1899, she married Robert Douglas, a saw miller, and for her own parents she gave the names of the grandparents who had raised her. Their daughter Janet was born in 1900. By 1911 she was raising the boy born Lawrence Brown as her son, Laurence B. Douglas, at 16 Lochrin Place. A woman who had been taken in took in a child.

Widowed in 1919, she worked as a school cleaner in Dunfermline. By 1929 she was using the surname Anderson, Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson of 39 Grieve Street, and both Janet and Laurence named her as their mother when they sailed for America. When and whom she remarried has not been found in the records.

lineage.who: John and Janet McDonald, her grandparents
Janet Page Douglas, 1900; Isabella Gray Douglas, died as an infant (family information)

name: Ann McDonald Hope
story: Ann McDonald was the mother of Elizabeth (Lizzie) McDonald, the woman who raised Laurence. She was about twenty and unmarried when Lizzie was born at Liberton in 1874. On July 28, 1876, she married Robert Alexander Hope, a laborer, at 33 Regent Park Square in Glasgow.

In 1878 Ann and Robert Hope sailed for New Zealand on assisted passages. Their son, John Rakaia Hope, was born at sea on September 26, 1878, and named for the emigrant ship. They settled at Cross Creek in the Wairarapa and raised four more children. Lizzie, four, stayed behind with her grandparents. Ann died at Cross Creek on January 13, 1915. These details come from family trees compiled by other researchers.

lineage.who: Elizabeth Millar McDonald, 1874; John Rakaia Hope, 1878, and four more

name: Robert Alexander Hope
story: Robert Alexander Hope married Ann McDonald, the mother of Lizzie Douglas, in Glasgow on July 28, 1876. He was born at Rigg, near Gretna, on July 14, 1852, the son of Gavin Hope and Elizabeth Millar.

In 1878 he and Ann emigrated to New Zealand, where their son John Rakaia Hope was born at sea. They settled at Cross Creek in the Wairarapa. Robert died at Pukekohe on December 3, 1930. Lizzie, Ann's daughter born before the marriage, was not taken with them.

lineage.who: John Rakaia Hope, 1878, and four more

name: John and Janet McDonald
story: John McDonald and his wife, Janet, born Janet Page, raised their granddaughter Lizzie, the woman who would raise Laurence. In 1881 the census found them on the Main Road at Gilmerton, south of Edinburgh, in the country of coal pits and miners' rows: John, fifty-two; Janet, fifty-two; their son George; a daughter, Janet; a son, Alexander; and Elizabeth, six, entered as Grandchild.

When Lizzie married Robert Douglas in 1899, she gave their names as her parents: John McDonald, coal salesman, and Janet McDonald, born Page. She named her first daughter Janet Page Douglas, after the grandmother who had raised her.

lineage.who: Ann McDonald (later Hope), George, Janet and Alexander
Elizabeth Millar McDonald (Lizzie Douglas), whom they raised

name: Archibald Douglas and Isabella Gray
story: Archibald Douglas and Isabella Gray were the parents of Robert Douglas, the man who raised Laurence. They married in January 1863 in the parish of Newton, on the southeastern edge of Edinburgh. When Robert was born in 1876 at 9 Canon Street, Archibald was a traveller for a wood merchant; by 1899 he was a forester.
Their names appear in Robert's birth, marriage and death entries. Family information says Robert and Lizzie named an infant daughter, Isabella Gray Douglas, for Robert's mother.

name: Janet Page Douglas Crombie
story: Janet Page Douglas was the daughter of Robert and Lizzie Douglas, and the sister Laurence grew up with. She was born in Edinburgh on April 29, 1900, seven years before him. In 1911 they were in the same house at Lochrin Place, and in August 1912 the Queen Anne School in Dunfermline admitted them two days apart from the same address.

She left school at fourteen in August 1914, and in 1921 she was a clerkess with the Dunfermline Co-operative Society. On July 16, 1926, she married Thomas Crombie, and that September they crossed into the United States at Detroit and settled on South Kostner Avenue in Chicago.

In May 1929 she came home to Dunfermline, and in September she sailed back with Laurence on the Duchess of Bedford. He lived as a lodger in her household in 1930, and it was her name Helen Harrison gave at the border as the friend she was joining. In 1936 Janet had twin daughters, Betty and Jessie. She became an American citizen in 1948 and died in December 1979, her last home Maywood, Illinois.

name: Thomas Crombie
story: Thomas Crombie was the husband of Janet Douglas, Laurence's sister. He was a man from Kinross, thirty-two when they married in Dunfermline on July 16, 1926. That September they crossed into the United States at Detroit and settled on the West Side of Chicago.

When Laurence arrived in 1929, he named Thomas, his brother-in-law, at 1534 South Kostner Avenue, as the person he was going to. On the 1930 census Thomas was the head of the house, a furniture salesman, with Laurence as his lodger. He became an American citizen on September 9, 1947.

name: Betty and Jessie Crombie
story: Elizabeth and Jessie Crombie were twin daughters of Janet and Thomas Crombie, born in Chicago on October 3, 1936. Elizabeth was called Betty. Their uncle Laurence was twenty-nine.
Jessie married Ronald H. Power in Cook County in September 1958. Betty died in Minneapolis on June 23, 2009, and Jessie at Poplar Grove, Illinois, on December 12, 2015.

name: Helen Ena Harrison
story: Helen Ena Harrison was Laurence's first wife. She was born at Bareilly, in British India, on June 26, 1907, twelve days after Laurence, the daughter of Richard Harrison, a colour sergeant in the 1st Battalion, Royal Scots Fusiliers, and Ada Elizabeth Townsend. She grew up with the regiment, in India and South Africa, and after the First World War the family settled in Ayr.

In September 1930 she sailed from Glasgow on the Athenia and crossed into the United States at Port Huron on September 15, naming as the friend she was joining Mrs. Janet Crombie of South Kostner Avenue, Chicago, Laurence's sister. Seven days later she and Laurence were married in Cook County. They lived at 1518 South Kostner Avenue. She went home to Scotland in 1934 and again from 1937 to 1938, and in May 1938 she named Laurence as her husband for the last time.

She divorced him; the date and court are not known. By 1950 she was a secretary for the National Coal Board in Ayr, and on August 11, 1950, she married George Lees Pirrie, a grocer's assistant. She died at 1a Inverkar Road, Ayr, on March 16, 1973, at sixty-five. Her death register lists both her husbands, the first as Laurence Brown Douglas.

lineage.who: Claud Richard, Frank Andrew and Alexander Edward Harrison

name: Captain Richard Harrison
story: Richard Harrison was the father of Helen Ena Harrison. He was born in Birmingham, England, about 1872, and went into the army. He married Ada Elizabeth Townsend in the Medway district in the spring of 1899. Their children were Claud Richard, born about 1904 at Aldershot; Helen Ena, born at Bareilly in 1907; Frank Andrew, born at Bareilly in 1908; and Alexander Edward, born in the Transvaal about January 1911.

In April 1911 he was a colour sergeant with the 1st Royal Scots Fusiliers at Roberts Heights, outside Pretoria. In 1914 he went to France with the battalion and was mentioned in despatches for Mons, the Marne and the Aisne. An R. Harrison of the regiment, very probably him, rose from the ranks to captain by 1919. After the war the family settled in Ayr, at Inverkar Road.

lineage.who: Claud Richard, Helen Ena, Frank Andrew and Alexander Edward Harrison

name: Ada Elizabeth Townsend Harrison
story: Ada Elizabeth Townsend was the mother of Helen Ena Harrison. She was the daughter of Andrew Isaac Townsend, an engine fitter at the Chatham naval dockyard, and grew up in Gillingham, Kent. In 1881, aged three, she was living with her parents at 9 Canterbury Street, New Brompton.

She married Richard Harrison in 1899 and followed the regiment to India and South Africa. After the war the family settled in Ayr. She died at 1a Inverkar Road, Ayr, on June 10, 1952, in the house where Helen and her second husband made their home.

lineage.who: Claud Richard, Helen Ena, Frank Andrew and Alexander Edward Harrison

name: Andrew Isaac Townsend
story: Andrew Isaac Townsend was Helen Harrison's grandfather. He was an engine fitter at the Chatham naval dockyard, twenty-nine in 1881, living at 9 Canterbury Street, New Brompton, with his wife, Ellen, and their daughter Ada, three. In 1901 Ada was back in her parents' house on Rock Avenue, Gillingham, while her husband was away with his regiment.
He died on January 31, 1937, at his daughter's house, 1 Inverkar Road, Ayr, three weeks after Helen sailed home to Scotland.

name: George Lees Pirrie
story: George Lees Pirrie was Helen Harrison's second husband. He was a grocer's assistant and a widower, thirty-six, living at 20 New Road, Ayr, when they married on August 11, 1950, by the forms of the Church of Scotland. His father was Andrew Pirrie, a journeyman bread baker, and his mother was Ann Lees.

He and Helen made their home at 1a Inverkar Road. When she died there in March 1973, he registered the death; by then he was a sales assistant in a department store. The register lists both her husbands, the first as Laurence Brown Douglas.

name: Constance Eugenie Darcy Douglas
story: Constance Eugenie Darcy was Laurence's wife for twenty-one years. She was born on Saturday, October 12, 1912, at 410 Smith Street, Providence, the first child of Albert Blake Darcy, a printer, and Eugenie Emma Delaire. Her parents later divorced, and she grew up between their households. She trained as a hairdresser, and in 1937 and 1938 she worked on Westminster Street, a block from Laurence's work on Weybosset Street.

On October 9, 1939, she and Laurence were married in Birmingham, Alabama. They lived in San Francisco, where he dressed windows for Bond Stores, then in the Pittsburgh district, and after the war in Pawtucket and Providence. She trained at the Rhode Island School of Practical Nursing, and by 1961 she was a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital.

Laurence died in 1961, when she was forty-eight. She kept nursing, worked eight years at Cranston General Hospital, and retired in 1974. In her last years she lived in East Greenwich. The family remembers her pleasant, congenial nature; her grandchildren called her Nan. She died on April 12, 1994, and was buried with Laurence at Saint Ann Cemetery, Cranston.

lineage.who: Three daughters: Eugenie, the eldest; Constance; and Norma, the youngest

name: Albert Blake Darcy
story: Albert Blake Darcy was the father of Constance, Laurence's wife. He was born on November 20, 1888, at Rumford, in East Providence, the first child of John F. and Maggie Darcy, whose family had come from Ireland. By 1910, at twenty-one, he was an apprentice on a Monotype machine, learning to set type.

On January 16, 1912, he married Eugenie Emma Delaire, seventeen. Their daughter Constance was born that October, and their son Albert Norman in 1915. He moved where the work was, to Boston and Taunton and back to Providence, where he set type for the Pawtucket Times and later the Providence Journal. The marriage ended in divorce; he married again, to Theresa B. Sullivan, and settled at Shawomet, in Warwick.

His mother, Margaret Jane Darcy, died at his house there in 1942. He died on November 4, 1957, sixteen days short of his sixty-ninth birthday, and was buried at Mount Saint Mary Cemetery in Pawtucket.

name: Eugenie Emma Delaire Darcy
story: Eugenie Emma Delaire was the mother of Constance, Laurence's wife. She was born at Sutton, Quebec, the daughter of Timothy and Julia Delaire, one of the many French Canadian families who came down to New England. She married Albert Blake Darcy in Providence on January 16, 1912, at seventeen. Her widowed mother, Julia, boarded with them on Smith Street the next year.

By 1930 she was divorced, the head of her own household at 111 Pratt Street, working as an interior decorator at a rug works. In the mid-1930s she and Constance shared a home, at Abbott Street and then Dartmouth Avenue. She died in 1966 and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston.

name: Albert Norman Darcy
story: Albert Norman Darcy was the younger brother of Constance, Laurence's wife. He was born at Taunton, Massachusetts, on December 7, 1915. On October 16, 1940, the same day Laurence registered for the draft in San Francisco, Albert signed his own draft card in Warwick, Rhode Island, and named his wife, Claire.
He died on October 1, 1954, aged thirty-eight, and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston, in section 5, lot 84. Laurence was buried in the same lot in 1961.
